rw: Dropout randomly ignores a share of neurons on each training step, which stops units from relying on each other and so reduces overfitting.

ww.Dropping rows with missing values from t: Dropping rows with missing values is data cleaning done before training, and it has nothing to do with switching off neurons inside the network during learning.
ww.Removing the last layer of the network p: Dropout does not delete the final layer for good; it only mutes random neurons temporarily during training, and the full network is used again when predicting.
ww.Stopping training when accuracy is perfe: Halting training when progress stalls is early stopping, a different regularization tool; dropout keeps training going while randomly silencing neurons, and it does not wait for perfect accuracy.

rw: An activation function takes a neuron's weighted inputs and produces its output, and its non-linear shape lets stacked layers learn patterns that a plain linear model cannot.

ww.A function that measures training time f: Time spent per pass over the data is measured by a timer or profiler; an activation function acts on each neuron's values and has no role in measuring duration.
ww.A function that splits the data into tra: Splitting data into training and test sets is a preprocessing step done before fitting; activation functions work inside the network on neuron values, not on whole data sets.
ww.A function that loads the data from a fi: Loading data from disk into memory is an input and output task handled by data loaders; activation functions only transform neuron values during the forward pass.

rw: ReLU returns max(0, x): a negative input such as -3 becomes 0, and a positive input such as 5 stays 5, which keeps computation cheap.

ww.Outputs the square of the input for ever: ReLU does not square anything; squaring would make large inputs grow quickly, while ReLU simply passes positive values through unchanged and sets negative ones to zero.
ww.Outputs a probability between 0 and 1 fo: Squashing any input into a probability between 0 and 1 describes the sigmoid function, whereas ReLU leaves positive values unbounded and does not produce probabilities.
ww.Outputs a random value between zero and: ReLU is fully deterministic; the same input always gives the same output, and no random number between zero and one is ever drawn by it.

rw: The sigmoid function 1 / (1 + e^-x) squeezes every real input into the open range between 0 and 1, which is why it is used for probabilities.

ww.Zero for negative inputs: Sigmoid does not output zero for negative inputs; a negative input such as -2 gives about 0.12, which is small but positive, so zero is wrong.
ww.A value from -10 to 10 only: Sigmoid outputs never leave the range from 0 to 1, so a range of -10 to 10 is wrong; that range is not what the function produces.
ww.The input unchanged: Returning the input unchanged is the identity function, which is a straight line; sigmoid bends the input into an S shape that stays between 0 and 1.

rw: A batch is a subset of the training examples fed through the network together, after which one update of the weights is computed from that group.

ww.A group of features used together as inp: Features are the input columns that describe each example; a batch is a group of examples, not a group of features, so this describes input variables instead.
ww.A group of models that are trained and c: Training several models and combining their predictions is called an ensemble; a batch is only a slice of the data used in a single weight update.
ww.The full set of test data held back to c: Test data held back for the final check is the test set; a batch comes from the training data and is used for learning, not for the final evaluation.

rw: One epoch is one pass through all the data, so 1,000 examples divided by a batch size of 100 gives 10 batches, each with 100 examples.

ww.100: 100 is the size of each batch, not the number of batches; dividing the 1,000 examples by 100 per batch gives 10 batches in one epoch.
ww.1,000: 1,000 is the total number of examples, not the number of batches; with 100 examples per batch the count must be smaller, namely 1,000 / 100 = 10.
ww.0.1: 0.1 would come from dividing 100 by 1,000, which flips the division; the number of batches is 1,000 / 100 = 10, and a count cannot be a fraction.

rw: Early stopping ends training once the validation score stops improving, which prevents the model from overfitting the training data as it keeps training for too long.

ww.Stopping data collection once enough row: Stopping data collection when enough rows are gathered is a sampling decision made before modelling; early stopping concerns when to end the training loop itself.
ww.Stopping the computer before training be: Halting the computer before training starts would leave a model that has learned nothing; early stopping happens during training, after the model has begun to learn.
ww.Stopping the model from making predictio: Early stopping does not block predictions on test data; the model still predicts on the test set, and the technique only decides when training should end.

rw: An RNN carries a hidden state from step to step, so it can use earlier items in a sequence, which suits text, speech and time series.

ww.Only still images, such as photos or sca: Still images such as photos are usually handled by convolutional networks; an RNN is built for ordered inputs, and the word only is also wrong here.
ww.Only tables with no order, such as a nam: Tables with no order are better suited to models like trees or feed-forward networks; an RNN gains its strength from the order of the data.
ww.Only audio recordings such as songs or c: Audio is one kind of sequence an RNN can process, but saying it handles only audio is false, since it also works well on text and time series.

rw: Attention lets the model assign weights to the parts of the input, so each output token can focus on the most relevant words, wherever they sit.

ww.A way to shorten the data by cutting row: Cutting rows from a table is data reduction, which has no link to attention; the attention mechanism works on the tokens inside the model, not on table records.
ww.A way to pay attention to the user, by s: Showing alerts and pop-up messages is a user interface feature; the attention in transformers is a mathematical weighting inside the model and has nothing to do with users.
ww.A way to store data on a disk, in files: Storing data in files and folders is file system work; transformer attention is a calculation that scores how much each input token matters, not a storage method.

rw: Tokenization splits text into smaller units, called tokens, such as words, sub-words or characters, which are then mapped to numbers the model can use.

ww.Counting characters only in a block of t: Counting characters only measures length; tokenization splits text into pieces such as words or sub-words so a model can process them, and counting is not splitting.
ww.Translating text from one language into: Translating text from one language to another is machine translation, a task a model performs; tokenization is only the earlier step of cutting text into units.
ww.Encrypting text so that only the key hol: Encrypting text with a key is a security method that hides content; tokenization does not hide anything, and its goal is to make text usable by models.

rw: The context window is the maximum amount of text, measured in tokens, that the model can take into account at one time, including both the prompt and its reply.

ww.The time a model takes to answer each us: The time to answer a question is latency; the context window is about how much text the model can read at once, not about speed.
ww.The window where the user types a questi: The place where a user types a question is the chat box or input field; the context window is a limit inside the model on the text it can use.
ww.The number of users who ask the model qu: The number of users asking questions is a measure of traffic or load; the context window is a size limit on the text for a single request.

rw: RLHF collects human judgments on which outputs are better, trains a reward model from them, and uses that reward signal to tune the model toward preferred behavior.

ww.Training a model without any data of any: RLHF depends on data, namely human preference ratings and sample outputs, so training with no data of any kind cannot be what it describes.
ww.Training a model to copy the human body: Copying how the human body moves is robotics or motion imitation; RLHF uses human feedback on text outputs as a reward, and has no concern with bodies.
ww.Training a model on its own outputs only: Training only on the model's own outputs with no person involved is the opposite of RLHF, which relies on human feedback to define what counts as a good output.

rw: Prompt injection is an attack where crafted text makes an AI system ignore its original instructions and do what the attacker wants instead, such as leaking data.

ww.A way to add data to a table in a databa: Adding rows to a database through a web form describes inserting records, and the similar sounding SQL injection attack, but it does not describe attacks on a language model's prompt.
ww.A medical injection given by a nurse to: A medical injection given by a nurse is a vaccination or treatment; the term here refers to a software security attack and has no medical meaning at all.
ww.A way to speed up a model by adding more: Adding chips and memory to servers is hardware scaling for speed; prompt injection is a security attack that manipulates the text given to a model.

rw: A guardrail is a rule, filter or check that limits harmful, unsafe or off-topic outputs, keeping the AI system within its intended and safe behavior.

ww.A fence around the data center to keep o: A fence around a data center is physical security; in AI a guardrail is a software rule or filter on model behavior, and it does not stop visitors.
ww.A way to make the model faster by using: Bigger chips would raise speed but not safety; a guardrail does not change how fast a model runs, only what the model is allowed to output.
ww.A tool that stores data in a table for l: Storing data in a table is database work; a guardrail does not store anything for staff and instead restricts or screens what the AI says.

rw: Zero-shot prompting gives the model only the task description and no worked examples, relying on what it already learned during its training to answer.

ww.Giving no instructions to the model abou: Zero-shot does not mean giving no instructions; the task is still described in the prompt, and what is missing is only worked examples of it.
ww.Training a model from scratch on a new d: Training from scratch on labeled data is ordinary supervised learning; zero-shot prompting uses an already trained model and changes nothing about its weights.
ww.Giving a model many examples of the task: Giving many examples in the prompt is few-shot or many-shot prompting; zero-shot has zero examples, which is the exact reverse of what this option says.

rw: Few-shot prompting places a small number of worked examples in the prompt, which shows the model the pattern and format of the task without any retraining.

ww.Asking the model a few times in a row to: Asking the same question several times in a row is repeated sampling; few-shot refers to the number of examples placed in the prompt, not repeats of the question.
ww.Giving no examples in the prompt, only a: Giving no examples and only a plain description is zero-shot prompting; few-shot means that a handful of examples, often two to five, are included.
ww.Retraining the model on thousands of exa: Retraining on thousands of examples is fine-tuning, which changes the model's weights; few-shot prompting leaves the weights alone and only adds examples to the prompt.

rw: Chain-of-thought prompting asks the model to work through the problem step by step before answering, which often improves results on math and logic questions.

ww.Chaining computers together in a network: Chaining computers into a network to share work is distributed computing; chain-of-thought is a prompting method about the model's own reasoning steps.
ww.Asking a model to answer instantly, with: Asking for an instant answer with no reasoning shown is the opposite of chain-of-thought, which deliberately asks for the intermediate steps to be written out.
ww.Linking many prompts in a row with no lo: Chain-of-thought is not about linking many prompts with no logic; it asks one model to reason through steps, and random linking would not improve any answer.

rw: Temperature controls randomness when sampling: a low value gives focused, predictable output, while a high value gives more varied and creative output.

ww.The size of the model in terms of the nu: The number of parameters measures model size, which is a separate property; temperature is a setting applied when the model chooses each next token.
ww.The speed of the internet link used by t: Internet speed in Mbps is a network property; temperature in a language model has no link to bandwidth and only affects how the output is sampled.
ww.The heat of the computer chips as the mo: The heat of chips is a hardware reading in degrees; the temperature setting in a language model is a sampling parameter and does not measure any physical heat.

rw: A vector database stores embeddings, which are lists of numbers capturing meaning, and quickly finds the nearest ones, supporting similarity search and retrieval for AI apps.

ww.Storing images only, such as photos and: Vector databases can hold more than images, and images alone is wrong; they store numeric embeddings of any content type so that similar items can be searched.
ww.Storing passwords for the accounts of a: Storing passwords is the job of a secrets manager or a credential vault; a vector database is built for similarity search over embeddings, not for security.
ww.Storing only numbers for spreadsheets in: Storing only numbers for spreadsheets describes an ordinary table or spreadsheet; a vector database indexes embeddings so that items with similar meaning can be found fast.

rw: Data labeling attaches tags or correct answers to raw data, such as marking images as cat or dog, so that supervised models can learn from examples.

ww.Encrypting data so that only approved us: Encrypting data so only approved users can read it is a security step; data labeling adds meaning to data and does not hide anything from users.
ww.Deleting old data from the tables so tha: Deleting old data to free disk space is data retention or cleanup; labeling adds information to data instead of removing any of it.
ww.Removing the names of columns from a tab: Removing column names from a table would make the data harder to use; labeling does the opposite by adding useful tags and answers to the data.

rw: Labels are the answers a model learns from, so mistakes in them teach it wrong patterns, which lowers accuracy and gives poor predictions on new data.

ww.Labels matter only for tables, not for i: Labels matter for images too, such as marking what an object is, so saying they matter only for tables is wrong; all supervised data depends on them.
ww.Labels make the data much smaller on dis: Labels add information to the data and do not shrink it; file size is unrelated to why label quality matters for what the model learns.
ww.Labels do not affect how models learn at: Labels directly decide what a supervised model learns, so they certainly affect learning; claiming they do not matter at all is plainly false.

rw: Oversampling increases the number of minority class examples, either by duplicating them or by creating synthetic ones, which helps balance an imbalanced data set.

ww.Removing examples of the common class on: Removing examples of the common class is undersampling, not oversampling; oversampling instead adds to the rare class so that both classes end up closer in size.
ww.Sampling less data from the large class: Taking less data from the large class is undersampling; oversampling goes the other way and increases the number of rare examples rather than shrinking the big class.
ww.Sampling every row twice at random to do: Sampling every row twice would double both classes and leave the imbalance unchanged; oversampling targets only the rare class so that the classes become more balanced.

rw: SMOTE creates synthetic minority class examples by interpolating between existing ones and their nearest neighbors, which helps balance classes without simply copying rows.

ww.A technique that scales features to a co: Scaling features to a common range is normalization or standardization; SMOTE does not rescale anything and instead creates new examples of the minority class.
ww.A technique that deletes outliers so the: Deleting outliers to move points toward the mean is outlier removal; SMOTE adds new minority points and does not delete any existing ones.
ww.A technique that compresses data files s: Compressing data files is storage work; SMOTE is a class balancing technique and does not change how much disk space the data takes.

rw: PCA finds new directions, called principal components, that capture the most variance in the data, so it can reduce the number of dimensions while keeping most information.

ww.A technique that labels data by hand, gi: Labeling data by hand is annotation, which gives examples tags; PCA is an unsupervised technique and needs no labels at all to find its directions.
ww.A technique that adds columns to a table: PCA does not add columns; it replaces many correlated columns with fewer new ones, whereas combining columns to add more is closer to feature engineering.
ww.A technique that sorts rows of a table b: Sorting rows by one column is simple ordering and leaves the data's dimensions unchanged; PCA instead creates new axes that capture variation across the columns.

rw: In k-means, k is the number of clusters; for example k = 3 asks the algorithm to split the points into three groups around three centers.

ww.The number of steps it takes: The number of steps is an iteration count; the letter k in k-means stands for how many clusters the algorithm should find, which is chosen in advance.
ww.The number of features used: The number of features is the dimension of the data and is not k; k only sets how many groups the algorithm will form.
ww.The number of rows in the table: The number of rows is the sample size; k is chosen independently of it, and it counts the clusters, not the records in the table.

rw: The elbow method plots error against k and picks the point where the drop slows sharply, which marks a sensible number of clusters for k-means.

ww.Choosing a chart color that makes the da: Choosing a chart color is a design matter; the elbow method is about picking the number of clusters by plotting error against k.
ww.Choosing a learning rate that sets the s: The learning rate is tuned with search or schedules; the elbow method looks at error against the number of clusters, not at update step size.
ww.Choosing a database system to store the: Choosing a database system is an engineering decision about storage; the elbow method is a clustering tool and has nothing to do with databases or keys.

rw: With k = 3, the algorithm finds the 3 training points closest to the new point and assigns the class that most of those 3 neighbors have.

ww.By the average of all points in the trai: Averaging all points in the training set ignores distance; kNN uses only the nearest few neighbors, and the vote is on classes, not an average of everything.
ww.By a random choice made by the computer: kNN is deterministic and uses distance to its neighbors; it does not choose randomly, so the same point gets the same class every time.
ww.By the class of the farthest point, as d: kNN looks at the closest points, not the farthest, because nearby points are the most similar; far points do not carry more weight, so this is backwards.

rw: Hyperparameter tuning tries different model settings, such as learning rate or tree depth, and keeps the combination that scores best on validation data.

ww.Searching the internet for data to add t: Searching the internet for data is data collection; hyperparameter search tries different settings such as learning rate or depth on the model that already exists.
ww.Searching for new features only, in the: Searching only for new features is feature engineering; tuning hyperparameters changes model settings such as tree depth, and does not look for columns of data.
ww.Searching for errors in code and fixing: Finding errors in code is debugging; hyperparameter tuning looks for the best model settings and does not fix any lines of code that fail.

rw: A baseline is a simple model, such as always predicting the average, that gives a reference score to compare against, showing whether a fancier model adds value.

ww.The most complex model that could be bui: A baseline is meant to be simple, not complex; the most complex model would be a poor yardstick, since the point is an easy reference to beat.
ww.The model with the highest cost of runni: Cost of running is unrelated to being a baseline; what defines it is simplicity and its role as the benchmark for comparison, not high expense.
ww.A model that has not been trained, so it: An untrained model produces meaningless output, so it is not a useful point of comparison; a baseline is a simple model that is actually fitted to the data.

rw: Naive Bayes applies Bayes' theorem and naively assumes that features are independent of each other given the class, which keeps it fast and simple.

ww.A classifier that works only on images a: Naive Bayes works well on text and numbers, so saying it handles only images is wrong; it is often used for spam filtering on text.
ww.A classifier that has no assumptions abo: Naive Bayes makes a strong assumption, namely that features are independent, so saying it has no assumptions is false; the word naive points to that assumption.
ww.A classifier that uses deep layers of no: Deep layers of nodes describe neural networks; naive Bayes is a simple probabilistic model built on Bayes' theorem and uses no layers of nodes.

rw: An SVM finds the boundary, called a hyperplane, that separates classes with the widest possible margin, which tends to generalize well on new data.

ww.A model that groups customers without la: Grouping customers without labels is clustering, an unsupervised task; an SVM is a supervised model that needs labeled classes to find its boundary.
ww.A model that predicts a number from a li: Predicting a number from a fitted line is linear regression; an SVM classifies by finding a boundary, though a variant can do regression.
ww.A model that stores data in a vector of: Storing data as a vector for a search is an embedding index; an SVM is a classification model that learns a decision boundary from labeled examples.

rw: Gradient boosting builds trees one after another, with each new tree fitted to the errors of the earlier ones, so the ensemble improves step by step.

ww.A method that increases the learning rat: Gradient boosting does not raise the learning rate each round; it adds new trees that fit the previous errors, and a rising rate would make training unstable.
ww.A method that boosts the speed of a GPU: Raising a GPU clock rate is overclocking, a hardware matter; gradient boosting is a machine learning method named for its way of fitting errors.
ww.A method that raises the prices of goods: Raising prices when demand grows is economics; gradient boosting is a machine learning ensemble method and has nothing to do with prices or markets.

rw: Bagging trains several models, each on a random sample of the data, then combines their predictions by voting or averaging, which lowers variance.

ww.Training one model many times without ch: Training one model many times on the same data gives identical results and no gain; bagging uses different random samples so the models differ and can be combined.
ww.Putting data in a bag, a container used: Putting data in a bag to carry papers is a literal reading of the word; bagging is short for bootstrap aggregating, a machine learning ensemble technique.
ww.Deleting data from a table that has gone: Deleting stale data to free room is data cleanup; bagging is an ensemble method that keeps data and trains models on random samples of it.

rw: R-squared is the share of the variation in the outcome that the model explains, running from 0 to 1, where higher means the model fits better.

ww.The average error of the model on the te: The average error on test data describes measures such as MAE or RMSE; R-squared is a proportion of variance explained, not an average mistake.
ww.The number of features used by the model: The number of features is the model's size or dimension and is not R-squared; R-squared reports how well the model explains the outcome.
ww.The learning rate used by the optimizer: The learning rate is an optimizer setting; R-squared is computed after fitting, to show how much of the outcome's variation the model accounts for.

rw: An R-squared of 0.85 means the model explains about 85 percent of the variation in the outcome, leaving about 15 percent unexplained by the model.

ww.The model is 85 percent accurate on ever: R-squared is not accuracy on every case; it describes explained variation, and it does not say that the model is right 85 percent of the time.
ww.The data has 85 rows, and each row has o: The number of rows has nothing to do with R-squared; the value 0.85 is a proportion of variance explained, not a count of data rows.
ww.The model is wrong 85 percent of the tim: An R-squared of 0.85 is a good fit, not a sign of being wrong 85 percent of the time; the model explains most variation.

rw: MSE takes the difference between each prediction and the actual value, squares it, and averages these squares, so larger errors are penalized more heavily.

ww.The largest error made by the model on a: The largest error on any case is the maximum error; MSE averages the squared errors over all cases and so it is not a single worst mistake.
ww.The average of the actual values in the: The average of the actual values is just the mean of the target; MSE instead averages the squared gaps between predictions and those actual values.
ww.The number of errors made by the model a: The number of errors is a count, such as in a misclassification tally; MSE measures the size of errors by squaring and averaging them, not how many occur.

rw: Substituting x = 5 gives y = 3 + 2(5) = 3 + 10 = 13, so the predicted value is 13.

ww.8: 8 comes from adding 3 and 5 and ignoring the slope of 2; substituting x = 5 into the equation gives 3 + 10 = 13.
ww.10: 10 comes from 2 times 5 and forgets the intercept of 3; the full prediction is 3 + 2(5) = 3 + 10 = 13.
ww.25: 25 comes from adding first and then multiplying, (3 + 2) x 5; the correct order of operations gives 3 + 2(5) = 13.

rw: The slope, here 2, shows how much y changes when x rises by one unit, so each extra unit of x adds 2 to the predicted y.

ww.The value of y when x is zero at start: The value of y when x is zero is the intercept, which is 3 here; the 2 is the slope instead and multiplies x.
ww.The error between a point and the line: The error between a point and the line is the residual; the coefficient 2 is a fixed part of the line's equation, not an error.
ww.The number of data points in the sample: The number of data points in the sample is the sample size n; the 2 in the equation is the slope and says nothing about the count.

rw: The 3 is the intercept, the predicted value of y when x equals zero, since y = 3 + 2(0) = 3.

ww.The number of rows in the data set: The number of rows is the sample size and is not found in the equation; the 3 is the intercept, which is the starting value of y.
ww.The change in y for each one-unit rise i: The change in y for each one-unit rise in x is the slope, which is 2 in this equation; the 3 is the intercept, not the slope.
ww.The error between a point and the line: The error between a point and the line is a residual, which differs for each point; the 3 is a constant that does not vary.

rw: Multicollinearity means that predictor variables are strongly correlated with one another, which makes regression coefficients unstable and their individual effects hard to separate.

ww.When there are too few features in the d: Too few features is a different problem, called underfitting or missing information; multicollinearity needs several features that are strongly related to each other.
ww.When the target is missing from many of: A target missing in many rows is a missing data problem; multicollinearity concerns relationships among the predictors, not gaps in the outcome column.
ww.When data is too large to fit into the m: Data too large for memory is a scaling problem; multicollinearity is about strong correlation between predictor variables and not about how big the data is.

rw: A residual equals the actual value minus the predicted value for a point, so it shows how far the fitted line misses that observation.

ww.The sum of all values in the data set, a: The sum of all values in the data set is just a total; a residual is a difference for a single point between what was observed and predicted.
ww.The number of predictors used in the reg: The number of predictors is the model's size; a residual is an error for one observation, so a count of predictors cannot be one.
ww.The slope of the line fitted through the: The slope of the fitted line is a coefficient of the model; a residual is the vertical gap between a point and that line.

rw: A learning curve plots model performance, such as error, against training set size or training time, which helps to diagnose underfitting and overfitting.

ww.A curve of the price of data over time a: The price of data over time is a market curve; a learning curve in machine learning plots model performance against training data size or training time.
ww.A curve showing how fast a person learns: A curve of how fast a person learns is a human learning curve; in machine learning the term refers to a model's performance as training grows.
ww.A curve showing company profits over a n: Company profits over the years is a financial chart; a machine learning learning curve is a plot of model scores against training size or time.

rw: Semi-supervised learning mixes a small set of labeled examples with a large pool of unlabeled data, which cuts the cost of labeling while still improving the model.

ww.Learning that a human supervises half th: Semi-supervised learning is about the mix of labeled and unlabeled data, not about a human supervising half the time while the machine works on the rest.
ww.Learning with no data at all, in which t: Learning with no data is impossible; semi-supervised learning uses data, a small labeled part plus a large unlabeled part, and does not guess answers alone.
ww.Learning only from labeled data, with no: Learning only from labeled data is supervised learning; semi-supervised learning also makes use of unlabeled data, so this option leaves out its defining feature.

rw: Self-supervised learning builds its own training signals from unlabeled data, for example by predicting a hidden word from its context, so no human labels are needed.

ww.Learning with no data at all, in which t: Learning with no data at all is impossible; self-supervised learning needs a large amount of unlabeled data from which it creates its own tasks.
ww.Learning with a teacher who grades every: A teacher who grades every answer describes supervised learning with labels; self-supervised learning produces its own targets from the data instead of relying on a grader.
ww.Learning from rewards only, with no data: Learning from rewards only describes reinforcement learning; self-supervised learning learns from patterns in the data itself and does not use a reward signal.

rw: A Markov decision process models decisions where the outcome depends on the current state and the action taken, and it forms the basis of reinforcement learning.

ww.Drawing charts from the rows of a table: Drawing charts from table rows is data visualization; a Markov decision process is a mathematical framework for sequential decisions and has no link to charts.
ww.Cleaning data by removing duplicates and: Cleaning data by removing duplicates is data preparation; a Markov decision process models states, actions and rewards, and does not clean any records.
ww.Encrypting files so that only approved u: Encrypting files is a security task; a Markov decision process is a model for decisions over time and has no role in protecting files with keys.

rw: The reward is a numeric signal from the environment that tells the agent how good its last action was, so the agent learns to earn more over time.

ww.A prize for the user who wins a game of: A prize for a game winner is an everyday meaning of reward; in reinforcement learning a reward is a numeric signal the environment gives to the agent.
ww.A tax paid by the agent to the state on: A tax paid to the state is a financial idea with nothing to do with learning; a reward is feedback the agent receives, not a payment it makes.
ww.A bonus paid to the programmer when the: A bonus paid to the programmer is a payroll matter; in reinforcement learning the reward goes to the learning agent as a signal, not to a person.

rw: The agent is the learner or decision maker that observes the environment, takes actions, and receives rewards, which lets it improve its behavior over time.

ww.The computer's operating system that run: The operating system runs the program but does not learn; the agent in reinforcement learning is the learner that chooses actions inside an environment.
ww.The dataset that the learner uses for tr: The data set used for training is not the agent; the agent is the actor that learns by acting and receiving rewards, rather than a data collection.
ww.The person who owns the data and the mod: The person who owns the data and model is the developer or owner; the agent is a software learner that acts in the environment.

rw: Per 100 people, 1 is sick and tests positive with 0.9, while 99 are healthy and 5 percent, about 4.95, test positive; 0.9 / 5.85 is about 15 percent.

ww.About 90 percent: 90 percent is the test's sensitivity, how often sick people test positive; it ignores that healthy people are far more numerous, so most positives are false alarms.
ww.About 50 percent: About 50 percent would need roughly equal true and false positives; here per 100 people 0.9 true positives face about 4.95 false ones, so it is far lower.
ww.About 1 percent: Positives are more common than the 1 percent base rate suggests; with 0.9 true and about 4.95 false positives per 100 people, the share is about 15 percent.

rw: Bayes' theorem lets you revise the probability of an event after seeing new evidence, by combining the prior probability with how likely the evidence is.

ww.Sort data into order from the smallest t: Putting data in order from smallest to largest is sorting; Bayes' theorem is a rule about conditional probabilities and does not order any values.
ww.Calculate the mean of any set of numbers: Calculating the mean is done by adding values and dividing by the count; Bayes' theorem concerns conditional probability and not averages of numbers.
ww.Predict the weather only, using satellit: Bayes' theorem applies to any event with conditional probabilities, including medical tests and spam, so limiting it to weather is wrong and far too narrow.

rw: A z-score tells how many standard deviations a value lies above or below the mean, which makes values from different scales comparable on one standard scale.

ww.The mean of a data set found by adding u: The mean found by adding values and dividing is the average, a different statistic; a z-score uses the mean and spread to place one value.
ww.The probability of an event, found as fa: Favorable outcomes over total outcomes is the classical definition of probability; a z-score is a standardized distance and not a probability.
ww.The size of the sample that was drawn fr: The size of a sample is the count n; a z-score describes where one observation sits relative to the mean and the standard deviation.

rw: The z-score is (value minus mean) divided by standard deviation, so (85 - 75) / 5 = 10 / 5 = 2 standard deviations above the mean.

ww.10: 10 is the raw difference 85 - 75 and is not divided by the standard deviation; the z-score is 10 / 5 = 2.
ww.15: 15 does not follow from the numbers; the z-score divides the difference of 10 by the standard deviation of 5, which gives 2.
ww.0.5: 0.5 comes from dividing 5 by 10, which turns the division upside down; the correct calculation is 10 / 5 = 2.

rw: The central limit theorem says that as sample size grows, the distribution of sample means approaches a normal distribution, whatever shape the population has.

ww.All data are normally distributed, whate: The central limit theorem does not say that all data are normal; it says the distribution of sample means becomes approximately normal, whatever the shape of the data.
ww.Samples must always be small, since larg: Larger samples give better, more precise estimates of the mean, so claiming that samples must be small is the opposite of what the theorem supports.
ww.The mean equals the median in every data: The mean equals the median only for symmetric data; skewed data sets have different values, and the theorem makes no such claim about every data set.

rw: The standard error of the mean is the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the mean, showing how much sample means vary around the true mean.

ww.The error made by a clerk in a data entr: A clerk's data entry error is a human mistake; the standard error of the mean is a statistic that describes how much sample means vary.
ww.The difference between two means found b: A difference between two means is found by subtraction and is a different quantity; the standard error describes the spread of a single mean across samples.
ww.The range of the data, found as the larg: The range is the maximum minus the minimum; the standard error of the mean is the standard deviation divided by the square root of n.

rw: A 95 percent confidence interval of 48 to 52 means we are fairly confident the true mean lies in that range, which is the usual practical reading.

ww.The true mean is certainly 50 and there: The interval does not prove that the true mean is exactly 50; it only gives a plausible range, and certainty is never claimed by a confidence interval.
ww.95 percent of individual values lie betw: The interval is about the mean, not about individual values; individual values spread much wider, so 95 percent of them need not lie in that range.
ww.The sample mean is 95 and the spread of: The 95 percent is the confidence level, not the sample mean; the sample mean is the center of the interval, here 50, and spread is not five units.

rw: A t-test compares means, for instance between two groups, and is used when the population variance is unknown, so the sample standard deviation stands in for it.

ww.Sorting data into order, from the smalle: Sorting data from smallest to largest is ordering and uses no test statistic; a t-test compares means to decide whether a difference is likely to be real.
ww.Cleaning data by removing duplicate rows: Cleaning data by removing duplicates is preparation done before analysis; a t-test is a hypothesis test and does not alter or clean the table.
ww.Drawing charts from the rows of a table: Drawing charts is visualization; a t-test is a statistical hypothesis test that produces a statistic and a p-value, not a chart of the rows.

rw: A chi-square test checks whether two categorical variables are related, by comparing observed counts in a table with the counts expected if they were independent.

ww.Comparing the means of two groups, using: Comparing the means of two groups is the job of a t-test; a chi-square test works with counts in categories and not with averages.
ww.Finding the median of a sorted set of nu: Finding the median is a descriptive calculation on ordered numbers; a chi-square test is an inferential test for categorical data and does not compute medians.
ww.Predicting a number from the other value: Predicting a number from other values is regression; a chi-square test does not predict anything and only tests for association between categories.

rw: ANOVA, or analysis of variance, compares the means of three or more groups at once, so it avoids running many separate t-tests that raise the error rate.

ww.Comparing only two means from two sample: Comparing only two means is the typical use of a t-test; ANOVA is designed for three or more groups, so limiting it to two is wrong.
ww.Cleaning data by removing errors and gap: Cleaning data by removing errors is a preparation step; ANOVA is a statistical test that compares group means and does not modify the data.
ww.Counting categories in a column of a tab: Counting categories in a column is a frequency count; ANOVA tests for differences between group means and does not tally categories of any column.

rw: Effect size measures how large a difference or relationship is, and not only whether one exists, which p-values alone cannot tell you about practical importance.

ww.The size of the sample, found by countin: Counting rows gives the sample size, which is not effect size; effect size shows how big a difference or relationship is, whatever the number of rows.
ww.The number of tests run on the data set: The number of tests run is a count of analyses and has no link to effect size, which measures the magnitude of a result.
ww.The size of a file that holds the data,: The size of a file in megabytes is a storage measure; effect size is a statistical idea about the magnitude of a result.

rw: With a huge sample even a tiny difference can reach statistical significance, so a very small p-value can accompany an effect too small to matter in practice.

ww.P-values measure importance, so a small: P-values do not measure importance; a small p-value only shows that data would be unlikely under the null, so it can go with a trivial effect.
ww.Small p-values are always meaningless, w: Small p-values are not meaningless; they can show real evidence of an effect, though their size does not tell you how large or important the effect is.
ww.Large samples never give small p-values,: Large samples make small p-values more likely, not less, because they detect tiny effects; so the claim that they never give small p-values is backwards.

rw: P-hacking means trying many analyses or subsets until a significant p-value appears and then reporting only that result, which inflates false positives.

ww.Cracking passwords by trying many guesse: Cracking passwords by guessing is a security attack; p-hacking is a research practice problem about misusing statistical analysis to reach significance.
ww.Reporting all results honestly, includin: Reporting all results honestly, including non-significant ones, is good practice and the opposite of p-hacking, which hides unsuccessful analyses and shows only the lucky one.
ww.Cleaning data by removing errors, gaps a: Cleaning data is a normal preparation step; p-hacking is the misuse of analysis choices to find a significant result, and it is not cleaning.

rw: Simpson's paradox is when a trend appearing in several groups reverses or disappears once the groups are combined, usually because of a lurking variable such as group size.

ww.A mistake in addition made when the numb: A mistake in hand addition is an arithmetic error; Simpson's paradox is a statistical effect where aggregation changes the direction of a trend.
ww.A trend that always holds true in every: A trend that holds in every group and in the whole is consistent and unremarkable; the paradox is precisely a case where the trend does not hold overall.
ww.A rule about samples that says how many: A rule about how many cases a study needs is sample size planning or power analysis; Simpson's paradox concerns reversed trends when data are combined.

rw: The number of orderings of 3 books is 3 factorial, which is 3 x 2 x 1 = 6.

ww.3: 3 counts only the choices for the first spot; arrangements of 3 books are 3 x 2 x 1, not just 3.
ww.9: 9 is 3 x 3 or 3 squared, which repeats choices; with no repeats the number of orders is 3 x 2 x 1 = 6.
ww.27: 27 is 3 x 3 x 3, which allows a book to be reused; each book is placed only once, so the answer is 3 x 2 x 1 = 6.

rw: The number of ways to choose 2 from 4 is C(4,2) = (4 x 3) / (2 x 1) = 6, because order does not matter.

ww.4: 4 is just the number of people and ignores pairs; choosing 2 of 4 is C(4,2) = (4 x 3) / 2 = 6.
ww.8: 8 is 4 x 2 and does not come from a combination formula; the correct count is C(4,2) = 4! / (2! x 2!) = 6.
ww.12: 12 is 4 x 3, which counts ordered pairs; since order does not matter each pair is counted twice, so divide by 2 to get 6.

rw: The expected value is the average of the equally likely outcomes, so (1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6) / 6 = 21 / 6 = 3.5.

ww.1: 1 is just the smallest face; the expected value averages all faces equally, giving (1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6) / 6 = 3.5.
ww.3: 3 is only a rounded or lower middle guess; the exact average of 1 through 6 is 21 / 6 = 3.5, which is not a whole number.
ww.6: 6 is the largest face and the maximum outcome, not the average; the expected value averages all six outcomes and equals 3.5.

rw: Variance is the average of the squared deviations from the mean, so it measures spread and is the square of the standard deviation.

ww.The average of the values in the whole d: The average of the values is the mean, a measure of center; variance measures spread by averaging squared distances from that mean instead.
ww.The middle value of the data after it is: The middle value after sorting is the median, another measure of center; variance describes how widely values are spread around the mean.
ww.The largest value minus the smallest, th: The largest value minus the smallest is the range, a simpler spread measure; variance averages squared deviations from the mean and uses every value.

rw: Variance is the square of the standard deviation, so with a standard deviation of 4 the variance is 4 x 4 = 16.

ww.2: 2 is the square root of 4, which goes in the wrong direction; variance squares the standard deviation, so 4 squared equals 16.
ww.4: 4 is the standard deviation itself; variance is its square, so 4 x 4 = 16 and not 4.
ww.8: 8 comes from doubling 4, but variance requires squaring the standard deviation, not doubling it; 4 squared is 16.

rw: A sampling distribution is the distribution of a statistic, such as the mean, calculated across many samples drawn from the same population, which shows its variability.

ww.A list of sample sizes used in each stud: A list of sample sizes is only a record of study design; a sampling distribution shows how a statistic such as the mean varies across many samples.
ww.A chart of the population showing the co: A chart of ages in the population is a population distribution; a sampling distribution is about a statistic computed from repeated samples, not about the population itself.
ww.The distribution of a single sample's va: The distribution of one sample's values is a sample distribution, a single sample's data; a sampling distribution is about a statistic across many different samples.

rw: Overfitting means the model learns noise and quirks of the training data, patterns that do not generalize, and so it does well in training but poorly on new data.

ww.Underfitting the model to the data: Underfitting is the opposite problem, where the model is too simple to capture the real pattern; fitting noise is called overfitting.
ww.Cross-validation on held-out folds: Cross-validation is a method for estimating performance on held-out folds and helps detect overfitting; it is not the name for fitting noise.
ww.Fitting the true signal only, to general: Fitting only the true signal so that it generalizes is the goal of good modeling; fitting noise is the opposite, which is overfitting.

rw: The list [4, 8, 15] has three items, and len returns the count of items, so len([4, 8, 15]) is 3.

ww.8: 8 is the middle element of the list, but len returns how many items there are, not the value of any item, so it returns 3.
ww.15: 15 is the last element of the list, but len gives the number of elements and not their values, so the answer is 3.
ww.27: 27 is not related to this list; len counts the items in it, and there are only three of them, so the answer is 3.

rw: sum adds all the items in the list, so 2 + 4 + 6 = 12.

ww.3: 3 is the number of items in the list, which is what len returns; sum adds the values, giving 2 + 4 + 6 = 12.
ww.6: 6 is only the last element of the list; sum adds every element, giving 2 + 4 + 6 = 12 and not a single item.
ww.48: 48 is the product 2 x 4 x 6, but sum adds values together instead of multiplying them; 2 + 4 + 6 = 12.

rw: The // operator performs floor division, so 7 divided by 2 is 3.5, which rounds down to 3.

ww.1: 1 is the remainder from 7 % 2, the modulo operator; the double slash // gives the quotient rounded down, which is 3.
ww.4: 4 would come from rounding 3.5 up, but floor division rounds down toward negative infinity, so 7 // 2 gives 3.
ww.3.5: 3.5 is the result of true division with a single slash, 7 / 2; the double slash // discards the fraction and returns 3.

rw: range(3) generates the integers 0, 1 and 2, starting from 0 and stopping before 3, so the loop prints those three values, each on its own line.

ww.Only 3, each on its own line: The loop prints each value of range(3), which starts at 0, so output is not only the number 3; range(3) stops before 3 and never produces it.
ww.0, 1, 2 and 3, each on its own line: range(3) stops before 3, so the loop does not print 3; it prints 0, 1 and 2 only, which is three lines rather than four.
ww.1, 2 and 3, each on its own line: range starts at 0 by default, not at 1, so the loop does not print 1, 2 and 3; the printed values are 0, 1 and 2.

rw: append adds the value 4 to the end of the list, so x becomes [1, 2, 3, 4] after the call.

ww.Prints 4 to the screen at once: append changes the list in place and prints nothing; printing needs a print call, so the code only adds 4 to the list and shows nothing.
ww.Replaces the list with just 4: append does not replace the list; the original items 1, 2 and 3 stay, and the list becomes [1, 2, 3, 4] after the call.
ww.Removes 4 from the list at once: append adds an item and never removes one; removing a value would require a method such as remove or pop, so 4 is added, not removed.

rw: By default df.head() shows the first five rows of the data frame, giving a quick preview of the data and its columns.

ww.The column names only, with no rows: The column names alone would come from df.columns; head shows actual rows of data, by default the first five, together with the column names.
ww.The last five rows of the data frame: The last five rows are shown by df.tail(); head shows the first five rows from the top of the data frame instead.
ww.A summary of statistics for each column: A summary of statistics for each column comes from df.describe(); head just displays the first five rows of raw data.

rw: df.describe() returns summary statistics, such as count, mean, standard deviation, minimum, quartiles and maximum, for each numeric column in the data frame.

ww.The first rows of the data frame, shown: The first rows of the data frame are shown by df.head(); describe computes summary statistics instead of displaying a preview of the raw rows.
ww.A chart of the numeric columns, drawn as: describe returns a table of numbers and does not draw a chart; charts need a plotting call such as df.plot() or a plotting library.
ww.The list of columns in the data frame, w: The list of columns with their types comes from df.info() or df.dtypes; describe summarizes the values with statistics and does not list data types.

rw: df.isnull() marks each missing cell as True, and sum() adds up the True values per column, which shows how many missing values each column has.

ww.The number of rows in the whole data fra: The number of rows is found with len(df) or df.shape; isnull().sum() counts missing values per column and does not give the total row count.
ww.The mean of each column in the table dat: The mean of each column comes from df.mean(); isnull().sum() counts empty cells and does not average any of the values in the table.
ww.The sum of all numbers in the data frame: The sum of all numbers would come from df.sum(); here isnull() first turns the cells into True or False, so sum counts missing cells instead.

rw: df.dropna() removes every row that contains at least one missing value by default, leaving only the complete rows in the data frame that is returned.

ww.Sorts the data by the values in a column: Sorting by a column is done with df.sort_values(); dropna deals with missing values and does not change the order of the rows.
ww.Adds missing values to the data frame ro: dropna removes missing values and does not add any; adding values to fill gaps would use methods such as fillna or interpolation instead.
ww.Fills missing values with zero in each r: Filling missing values with zero is the job of df.fillna(0); dropna drops rows with missing values and does not fill anything in.

rw: groupby splits the rows by region, selects the sales column, and sum adds the sales within each region, giving total sales for each region.

ww.The count of all regions: The count of regions would use count or nunique; this code groups rows by region and adds up the sales column inside each group.
ww.The mean sales for all regions: The mean sales would need .mean() instead of .sum(); the call here adds up the sales in each region and does not average them.
ww.A list of all the regions: A list of all the regions would come from df['region'].unique(); this expression adds numbers and returns totals, not a list of region names.

rw: An INNER JOIN returns only the rows where the join condition finds matching values in both tables, and it drops rows that lack a match on either side.

ww.All rows from both tables, matched or no: Returning all rows from both tables, matched or not, describes a FULL OUTER JOIN; an INNER JOIN keeps only rows that match in both tables.
ww.Only rows without matches in either tabl: Rows without matches in either table are what an INNER JOIN leaves out; it returns only the rows that have a match in both.
ww.All rows from the left table only, match: All rows from the left table is a LEFT JOIN; an INNER JOIN also drops left rows that have no match in the right table.

rw: A LEFT JOIN returns every row from the left table plus matching rows from the right, with NULL values for left rows that have no match.

ww.No rows at all from either of the two ta: A join between two tables does return rows when matches exist; returning no rows at all from either table is not what a LEFT JOIN does.
ww.Only rows that match in both tables, wit: Only rows matching in both tables is an INNER JOIN; a LEFT JOIN keeps unmatched left rows too, filling the right side with NULL values.
ww.All rows from the right table only, whet: All rows from the right table only is a RIGHT JOIN; a LEFT JOIN keeps all rows from the left table, not the right.

rw: HAVING filters groups after aggregation, for example keeping only regions where SUM(sales) exceeds 1000, which WHERE cannot do since it runs before grouping.

ww.Filters rows before grouping: Filtering rows before grouping is the job of the WHERE clause; HAVING runs after GROUP BY and so cannot be what filters rows first.
ww.Sorts the results of a query: Sorting the results of a query is done with ORDER BY; HAVING does not sort and only filters groups after aggregation has been done.
ww.Joins tables on a shared column: Joining tables on a shared column is done with JOIN and ON; HAVING is a filter on grouped results and does not combine tables.

rw: AVG returns the average of the values in a numeric column, found by adding the values and dividing by their count.

ww.COUNT: COUNT returns how many rows or values there are, not their average; the average of a numeric column needs AVG.
ww.SUM: SUM adds the values of a column to give a total, but does not divide by the count, so it is not the average.
ww.MAX: MAX returns the largest value in the column, not the average; the function that computes the mean of the values is AVG.

rw: SELECT DISTINCT city returns each different city once, removing repeated values, so the result is a list of unique cities.

ww.The largest city listed: The largest value would come from MAX; DISTINCT removes repeated values, so this query returns each city only once and not the largest one.
ww.The count of cities: The count of cities would need COUNT(DISTINCT city); this query returns the city names themselves, once each, and does not count them.
ww.All cities with repeats: All cities with repeats is what plain SELECT city returns; the DISTINCT keyword is there to remove those repeated values.

rw: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders; is valid SQL that counts all the rows in the orders table, using COUNT(*) in the select list and the table after FROM.

ww.SELECT orders FROM COUNT;: The syntax is wrong, because COUNT is a function and not a table and cannot follow FROM; the table orders must come after FROM.
ww.SELECT orders COUNT(*) FROM;: The order of words is invalid, since the function COUNT(*) must be a selected expression and FROM must be followed by the table name orders.
ww.SELECT SUM(*) FROM orders;: SUM(*) is not valid because SUM needs a numeric column to add; counting rows takes COUNT(*), which counts every row in the table.

rw: Normalization organizes tables so each fact is stored once, which reduces duplicate data and avoids update errors across the database.

ww.Encrypting data so only users can read i: Encrypting data so only users can read it is security; normalization in a database is about how tables are organized, and does not hide data.
ww.Deleting old data from the tables each y: Deleting old data each year is data retention; normalization restructures tables to remove repetition and does not delete records because they are old.
ww.Scaling numeric values to a common range: Scaling numeric values to a common range is feature scaling in machine learning; database normalization concerns table design and removing redundancy, which is a different idea.

rw: An index is a data structure, like a book's index, that lets the database find rows by a column's values quickly instead of scanning the whole table.

ww.A chart that plots the values of one col: A chart that plots a column is a visualization; a database index is a hidden lookup structure and is not drawn for the user.
ww.A list of users who may access the table: A list of users who may access the table is a permissions or access control list; an index only speeds up searches and controls no access.
ww.A backup copy of the table kept on a ser: A backup copy kept on a server is a backup; an index is a lookup structure built from the table and does not preserve the data.

rw: A data lake is a large store holding raw data in many formats, such as files, logs and images, which is kept until needed for analysis.

ww.A small database of clean tables in one: A small database of clean tables in one file describes a simple database like SQLite; a data lake is large and holds raw, varied data.
ww.A physical lake where fish live and boat: A physical lake with fish and boats is the everyday meaning of the word; in data work the term names a storage system, not a place.
ww.A chart that shows many values over time: A chart showing many values over time is a visualization, such as a line chart; a data lake is a storage system and not a graphic.

rw: Data governance is the set of policies and processes that manage data quality, security and proper use across an organization, defining who may do what with data.

ww.Writing code in a programming language t: Writing code to build apps is software development; data governance is about managing data and the rules for it, not programming.
ww.Making charts and graphs from a data set: Making charts from a data set is data visualization; governance sets policies for data and does not draw any graphs to show patterns.
ww.Cleaning a screen with a soft cloth so t: Cleaning a screen with a cloth is a hardware chore; data governance is an organizational practice for handling data and has no link to screens.

rw: Data lineage is a record of where data came from and how it was changed along the way, which helps trace errors and prove trust.

ww.The size of a file that holds the data i: The size of a file in megabytes is a storage measure; lineage is a history of the data's origin and transformations and not its size.
ww.The speed of a query that runs on a data: The speed of a query is a performance measure; lineage tracks the path data took and what happened to it, not how fast queries run.
ww.A list of family trees drawn up by a his: A list of family trees by a historian is genealogy; in data work lineage means the data's own origin and change history.

rw: A data catalog is an organized inventory of data assets with descriptions, so users can search for data sets and understand what each one contains.

ww.A mail-order list of goods that a firm s: A mail-order list of goods is a product catalog sold by post; a data catalog lists data assets and not products for sale.
ww.A list of passwords kept by the staff of: A list of passwords is a security risk and a credential store; a data catalog describes data sets so people can find and understand them.
ww.A chart that shows how many assets a fir: A chart of how many assets a firm holds is a visualization; a data catalog is a searchable inventory with descriptions and not a graphic.

rw: A stakeholder-ready chart is clear, accurately scaled, properly labeled and answers the audience's question, so decision makers can read it correctly without extra explanation.

ww.One with as many colors as possible, so: Using as many colors as possible clutters a chart and makes it harder to read; a good stakeholder chart uses color sparingly and with purpose.
ww.One with no labels, no title and no scal: A chart with no labels, title or scale leaves the viewer guessing, which defeats its purpose; a stakeholder-ready chart explains itself and answers a clear question.
ww.One that hides the axis and the scale so: Hiding the axis and the scale stops readers from judging sizes and can mislead them; a stakeholder-ready chart shows axes honestly.

rw: The line inside the box of a box plot marks the median, the middle value of the data, with half the values above it and half below.

ww.The maximum: The maximum is shown by the end of the upper whisker, or by points above it; the line inside the box marks the middle of the data.
ww.The mode: A box plot does not show the mode, the most frequent value; the line inside the box marks the median instead.
ww.The mean: The mean is not displayed by the standard line in a box plot; that line marks the median, though some plots add a separate marker for the mean.

rw: Points beyond the whiskers usually indicate potential outliers, values unusually far from the bulk of the data, often beyond 1.5 times the interquartile range.

ww.Errors in data overall: Points beyond the whiskers are flagged as unusual values, not necessarily errors; they may be real data, so calling them errors overall is too strong.
ww.The mean value: The mean value is not marked by such points; they lie far from the box and show unusual values, not the center of the data.
ww.Missing values: Missing values have no position and cannot be plotted as points; the points beyond the whiskers are actual observations that are unusually high or low.

rw: When y tends to rise as x rises, the cloud slopes upward, which shows a positive relationship or correlation between the two variables.

ww.A perfect circle of dots on the whole pl: A perfect circle of dots would be a special pattern; an upward-sloping cloud shows that the variables rise together, not a circular shape.
ww.No relationship between the two variable: No relationship would show as a shapeless cloud with no slope; an upward-sloping cloud has a clear direction, so a relationship exists.
ww.A negative relationship between the vari: A negative relationship shows as a cloud sloping downward, where y falls as x rises; an upward slope shows the opposite, a positive relationship.

rw: Labeled axes and units tell readers what is being measured and in what scale, so they can interpret the values correctly instead of guessing.

ww.Labels slow the chart and make it harder: Labels do not slow a chart or make it harder to read; they make it easier to understand, and clear labeling is standard good practice.
ww.Labels are never needed on any kind of c: Labels are needed on almost every chart, because without them readers cannot tell what the numbers mean, so the claim that they are never needed is wrong.
ww.Labels hide the data behind the text on: Axis labels sit outside the plotted area and do not cover the data; a chart with clear labels shows the data and its meaning together.

rw: With many small categories the slices become thin and similar in size, so it is hard to compare them by eye, and a bar chart works better.

ww.Pie charts cannot show shares: Pie charts do show shares of a whole, which is their purpose; the problem with many small categories is readability, not an inability to show shares.
ww.Pie charts use too much ink: Ink use is not the main concern; the real issue is that many thin slices are hard to read and compare, not how much ink is used.
ww.Pie charts are illegal in print: Pie charts are legal in print and are used widely; the weakness with many categories is that tiny slices are difficult to tell apart.

rw: Overplotting happens when so many points overlap that individual points and patterns are hidden, which can be eased with transparency, smaller points or sampling.

ww.Plotting offline, without a network conn: Plotting offline has nothing to do with the layout of points; overplotting is a visual problem of crowded points hiding each other on the chart.
ww.Plotting in the wrong color, so points a: Using the wrong color is a styling problem; overplotting is specifically about points piling on top of each other and hiding the density underneath.
ww.Plotting too few points to see any patte: Too few points is the opposite problem; overplotting comes from having too many points crowded together, not from a lack of data.

rw: Differential privacy adds carefully calibrated random noise to data or results, so the output barely changes whether or not any one person is included, protecting individuals.

ww.A method for comparing two people on the: Comparing two people on pay and records is an ordinary analysis task; differential privacy is a mathematical privacy guarantee about releasing results, not a comparison method.
ww.A way of deleting files from a disk so t: Deleting files so that they cannot be restored is secure erasure; differential privacy protects people inside data that is still being used and shared.
ww.A way of hiding a firm's profits from th: Hiding a firm's profits from the tax agency would be tax evasion; differential privacy is a legitimate method for protecting individuals' data in published results.

rw: Federated learning trains a shared model across many devices, each using its local data, and only model updates are sent back, so raw data never leaves the device.

ww.Training a model on one computer in a si: Training on one computer in a single room with all the data kept there is centralized training, the opposite of federated learning's distributed approach.
ww.Training with government data only, kept: Government data on a single computer in a secure room is again centralized; federated learning spreads training over many devices and keeps raw data where it is.
ww.Training with no data at all, so that th: Training needs data, so training with none at all cannot work; federated learning uses real data that stays on each user's own device.

rw: A model card is a document describing a model's purpose, performance, limits and intended use, which helps users judge whether and how to use it responsibly.

ww.A credit card for models, used to pay fo: A credit card for paying computing time is a payment product; a model card is documentation and has nothing to do with money or billing.
ww.A greeting card sent to a model's creato: A greeting card sent to creators is a social gesture; in AI a model card is a structured document that describes a model for users.
ww.A list of passwords used by the model to: A list of passwords the model uses to log in would be a serious security leak; a model card is public documentation and never holds credentials.
